paragraphs.text: For centuries, mapmakers copied details from earlier maps rather than visiting the places themselves. As a result, mistakes could survive for hundreds of years. One of the best known is the belief that California was an island, which appeared on European maps from the early 1600s.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The error probably began with a single account of a sea voyage and spread because printed maps were copied widely. Even after explorers travelled overland from Mexico to California in the late 1600s, many publishers continued to show the island, partly because engraving a new copper plate was expensive.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Mistakes did not only affect coastlines. Some maps showed mountain ranges that did not exist. One of these, the Mountains of Kong in West Africa, remained on maps for about a century before a French expedition in the 1880s reported that there were no mountains there.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Today’s digital maps are updated far more often, but they are not free from error. In 2012 researchers noticed a small island in the Pacific that appeared on several online maps but had never been seen by ships passing the area. It was removed after a survey vessel sailed through the empty sea where it was supposed to be.
paragraphs.label: D

items.prompt: Mapmakers in the past often relied on earlier maps instead of their own travels.
The idea that California was an island first appeared on Spanish maps.
Publishers stopped showing California as an island as soon as the overland journey had been made.
The Mountains of Kong were shown on maps for around one hundred years.
Several ships had reported the Pacific island before 2012.
